title: Cells and Viruses
seo_title: Life Sciences 11: Cells and Viruses Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Life is a result of interactions at the molecular and cellular levels: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelles, the cell membrane and transport, microscopy, and viruses. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Life Sciences 11)
meta_desc: Free Life Sciences 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): cells, organelles, membranes and viruses. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; eukaryotes do.
body_html:
How to think about it

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts, ribosomes, the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

Viruses are not cells: they are genetic material in a protein coat. They can reproduce only inside a host cell, using the lytic or lysogenic cycle. Antibiotics do not work against viruses; vaccines help the immune system fight them.

Example

Which organelle makes proteins?

Small, found on the rough ER

Answer: the ribosome

Example

Why are viruses not considered living by many scientists?

Can they reproduce alone?

Answer: they cannot reproduce or use energy on their own

Common mistakes

  • Thinking bacteria have a nucleus.
  • Mixing up diffusion and active transport.
  • Thinking antibiotics kill viruses.

items.q: In a photograph a mitochondrion is 80.0 mm long. The magnification is ×20000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 80.0 mm ÷ 20000 = 0.00400 mm = 4.00 µm.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −400 kPa and the sucrose solution has −1000 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
